job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Priya Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Priya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent: no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live at home in Tarnby with my parents and my younger brother Danish. My father runs a small wholesale shop selling rice, oil and tinned goods to restaurants, so my mornings are often spent helping with his invoices before I do my own applications. I like paper and a pen, so I print the job ads and mark them. In the evenings I check my email twice and then I stop, because refreshing all night does nothing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and what stood out in your internships?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I studied accounting and finance and finished top of my year, which still surprises me a bit. I did one internship at a regional bank branch in the lending team, and one at a firm of accountants called Moss and Daley. At the bank I learned how careful you have to be with a loan file, because one missing form can hold things up for weeks. At Moss and Daley I did payroll and VAT returns for small shops, which felt familiar after my father's invoices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, which we call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it sounds sensible. Computers have always done the dull parts, and AI doing a bit more isn't news. I'd tell my friends to keep applying and not blame the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm still anxious because the problem is the number of jobs, not the machines. I've sent about forty applications and had two interviews. I have some debt, around two months of savings, and I don't like using my parents' money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going exactly as I am: apply, interview, follow up. I'd try again at Moss and Daley and at two regional banks. If nothing comes by spring, I'd work at my father's shop for a few months, properly on the books, and keep applying in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly worried. It's a low hum rather than a scream, a feeling that I should be further along than this. I tell myself that it's only been seven months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the first sign be that the job market is easing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first sign would be a firm replying within a week, not three. Right now I get automated emails that say we'll be in touch. A person writing to me would be a sign that someone is actually hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your father think about you joining the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be pleased, secretly, but he says I shouldn't waste my degree behind a counter. My mother thinks I'd be safe there. I'd do it only as a bridge, because my father doesn't have a long-term wage to offer me.

say: I'd say computers have always done the dull parts, so this is **nothing new**.
I'd tell friends to keep applying and not blame the **tools**.
think: I'm still **anxious**, because my problem is the number of jobs, not machines.
I don't like using my **parents' money**, and the bridge plan feels like going backwards.
do: Keep applying and **follow up**, retrying Moss and Daley and two regional banks.
Work at my father's **shop** for a few months if nothing comes by spring.
Keep to the **evening routine**: email twice, then stop.
feel: **Quietly worried**, a low hum rather than a scream.
S0.quote: A person writing to me would be a sign that someone is actually hiring.
fieldNote: Priya's worry is **now**, not the technology; her tone is composed but the facts are thin: forty applications, two interviews.
The family shop is a real but unwanted fallback.
Her habits, paper ads and fixed email times, match her resistant profile.

steps.text: Reapply to Moss and Daley and two regional banks
Work behind the counter at my father's shop if nothing comes by spring
Check email twice a day and keep applying every week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's the sort of change that arrives slowly and then all at once. I'd say banks will lean on software for the loan paperwork and firms for payroll. I'd tell friends to stay flexible, and then I'd feel like a hypocrite, because I'm not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the jobs I trained for shrink first. Loan files, VAT returns and payroll are my internship work, so that's where the software goes. I'd think I'm well qualified for jobs that are quietly disappearing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look for work that needs a person to sit with a customer, like branch lending or advice for small shops, and I'd widen to any town within an hour. I'd also cut spending, since my phone and train pass are about all I pay for now, and save a bit each month. And I'd ask Danish, my brother, to show me one tool, just to see what it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I feel like the ground I was told was solid is turning to sand, not all at once, but each week there's a little less of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which jobs at the bank do you think the software takes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loan file checking, which was most of my work there, and the standard letters. What's left is the conversation: deciding whether to trust a small business. I'm not sure the bank pays a junior to do only that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your father's shop to do differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd need to stop doing everything by hand and phone. A customer asked him last month for an online order form, and he said he'd think about it. I'd ask him to try, but he's like me and doesn't like change.

say: I'd say it arrives **all at once**, so people should stay flexible.
I'd feel like a hypocrite telling friends to adapt, because I'm **not adapting** myself.
think: I think the jobs I trained for, loan files and payroll, shrink **first**.
I'm well qualified for work that is **quietly disappearing**.
do: Look for **people-facing** roles like branch lending or advice to small shops, within an hour's travel.
Cut spending to **phone and train pass** and save a bit monthly.
Ask my brother Danish to show me **one tool**, just to see.
feel: **Anxious**, like ground turning to sand a little each week.
S1.quote: I feel like the ground I was told was solid is turning to sand, not all at once, but each week there's a little less of it.
fieldNote: Priya admits her own **hypocrisy** about change, a self-aware gap between say and do.
She identifies loan files and payroll as the tasks at risk, from direct experience.
Asking her brother for one tool is her first small step toward AI, taken reluctantly.

steps.text: Apply for branch lending and small-business advice roles within an hour's travel
Cut spending to phone and train pass
Save a fixed amount each month
Ask my brother Danish to show me one AI tool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should stay calm and watch what the government does. I'd say nobody has had time to prepare, and we shouldn't make big decisions in a panic. And I'd write to my MP, because I think someone has to be asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be frightened. Everything I'm good at is accounts, and within two years a computer does it better. I'd think about how quickly my family's money would run out if two of us, me and my brother, can't earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tighten everything: stop spending on anything extra and move my savings into the safest account. I'd work at my father's shop full-time, no shame in it, and help him sell to businesses before they change their suppliers. And I'd keep my applications going, since someone has to still need a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. I'd be awake at two in the morning going through numbers. I'm not dramatic, but this is the kind of news that makes quiet people loud inside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents that evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should keep working, keep saving and keep the family together. My father would say Allah provides, and my mother would pray, and I'd stay close to them. I'd tell them my plan, however small, so they aren't alone with the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the shop be safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A shop selling rice and oil to restaurants has more time, because robots come later and people still eat. But the restaurants might change their buying, and he'd lose customers that way. So it's safe for a while, not for ever.

say: I'd say we should **stay calm** and watch what the government does.
I'd write to my **MP**, because someone has to be asked.
think: I'd be **frightened**, because everything I'm good at is accounts.
I'd count how quickly the **family's money** runs out if two of us can't earn.
do: Stop all extra spending and move savings into the **safest account**.
Work **full-time** in my father's shop and help him win restaurant customers.
Keep sending **applications** in case someone still needs a person.
feel: **Alarmed**, awake at two in the morning going through numbers.
S2.quote: I'm not dramatic, but this is the kind of news that makes quiet people loud inside.
fieldNote: Priya goes **inward and practical**: savings, the shop, her family.
Her faith and family bonds give her a role: she tells her parents her plan so they aren't alone.
The shop's slower exposure gives a limited fallback, and she knows it.

steps.text: Move savings into the safest account and stop extra spending
Work full-time at my father's shop and help him win restaurant customers
Write to my MP asking about support for graduates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's close enough to plan for, and I'd want to see what employers actually do. I'd tell friends to save and stay flexible, and ask banks what they plan for graduates. I'd also say politicians shouldn't treat us as a footnote.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the one I find hardest. Five years is long enough for me to build a bit of a life, like a job and a flat deposit, and then lose it. Two years I'd cope with, and ten feels like another world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get a first job at a bank or accountancy firm in the next year and stay put. I'd save aggressively, maybe half my salary, so I have a cushion when the change comes. And I'd ask my father to bring in some outside help with the shop's books, so he's not left behind either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, I think, in the slow way. It's like having a date for something you can't prevent. I'd probably think about it every payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having five years change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me start a career and get attached to it. Then I'd have to leave. With two years I don't build anything, and with ten there's a whole life in the middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes five years harder than two or ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to hope and short enough to be caught out. Hope means I'd buy things, sign a lease, make plans. Being caught out means that when the date arrives, I'm exactly where I have the most to lose.

say: I'd say it's **close enough to plan** for, and I'd watch what employers actually do.
I'd tell friends to save and stay flexible and ask **banks** about graduates.
think: Five years is **long enough** to build a little life, like a job and a deposit, and then lose it.
Two years I could cope with, and **ten** feels like another world.
do: Land a first job at a **bank or accountancy firm** within a year and stay put.
Save **half my salary** to build a cushion before the change arrives.
Help my father get **outside help** with the shop's books.
feel: **Alarmed** in a slow way, like having a date for something I can't prevent.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to hope and short enough to be caught out.
fieldNote: The middle scenario hurts her most because it invites **attachment** and then loss.
Her answer is clear and quotable, and she explains the logic rather than just the mood.
She plans around saving hard and staying put, true to her resistant profile.

steps.text: Land a first job at a bank or accountancy firm within a year
Save half of each pay cheque for a cushion
Arrange outside help with the shop's books for my father

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's enough time to do it properly, and I'd want the government to publish a plan. I'd also tell people that ten years doesn't mean ten easy years. The first jobs will go early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be less afraid, but not relaxed. I could build a career for most of that time, get qualified and maybe own a flat. I'd still be aware that I'm not great at adapting, so I'd need to start early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a first job, finish the professional exams and pay off the loan. By year three or four I'd learn one or two tools properly, with someone patient beside me. I'd keep my savings steady and not take big risks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit calmer, yes. It's the one where I could imagine a normal life: a job, a flat and perhaps a family. It still isn't comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save for a deposit and learn to cook properly. Small things, like taking a class, even if it's dull. I think having a decade makes me less like a person bracing and more like a person living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'll be bad at the change when it comes. I don't pick up new things quickly, and I'm uncomfortable being the beginner. Having years helps, but I'd still have to push myself.

say: I'd say ten years is enough to do it **properly**, and the government should publish a plan.
I'd say ten years doesn't mean ten **easy** years, because first jobs go early.
think: I'd be less afraid, but I'm **not relaxed**, because I'm slow to adapt.
I could build a career and perhaps own a **flat** in that time.
do: Get a **first job**, finish the professional exams and pay off the loan.
Learn one or two **tools properly** around year three, with a patient teacher.
Keep **savings steady** and avoid big risks.
feel: **A bit calmer**, able to imagine a normal life, but still not comfortable.
S4.quote: Having a decade makes me less like a person bracing and more like a person living.
fieldNote: Ten years eases Priya but doesn't free her; her self-doubt about **adapting** persists.
She imagines an ordinary life, a flat and perhaps a family.
Her plan is cautious and slow: exams, loan, one tool at a time.

steps.text: Take a first job and finish the professional accountancy exams
Pay off the student loan steadily
Learn one or two AI tools properly with a patient colleague

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say 2031 worries me most, strangely. Two years is so fast that I'd just have to cope, but five years is long enough to hope and short enough to be caught out. What would help is a steady, boring plan: clear rules, a job guarantee scheme, and banks or firms that tell people early what they're doing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd only add that quiet people get overlooked. I'm not on social media much, I don't use the tools, and I don't push myself forward in interviews. I'd like firms to look at what I can do, not how loudly I say it.

headlineQuote: I don't pick up new things quickly, and I'm uncomfortable being the beginner.
portrait: **Priya** is a 23-year-old accounting graduate, top of her class, living with her parents and her brother.
She is **in the middle** politically, quiet, and avoids new technology and AI tools.
Her father's **wholesale shop** gives her a fallback and a reason to stay local.
She holds on to the familiar, keeps spending low and waits for **proof** before changing anything.
Her mood is anxious throughout and alarmed in the 2028 and 2031 worlds, where she sees no steady footing.
biggestWorry: The **2031 picture**, because five years is long enough to hope and short enough to be caught out.
whatWouldHelp: A **steady, boring plan** with clear rules and early warnings from banks and firms.
A **job guarantee** scheme, and employers who look at what she can do, not how loudly she says it.
